units.title: Unit 17 — The place where you live
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 17. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Describe where a home is located, including the centre of town and the outskirts.
Contrast used to live with a present home and explain moving house.
Distinguish owning from renting and flat from apartment.
Describe building features, floors, stairs, lifts, balconies and air conditioning.
Describe rural homes using cottage, charming, character, dark, light and central heating.
Use British English floor numbering and appropriate location prepositions.

items.example: The new library is in a convenient location.
items.note: A place or position, especially when describing where a home is situated.

items.example: The outskirts are quieter than the city centre.
items.note: The outer areas of a town or city; normally plural.

items.example: They found an affordable house on the outskirts of town.
items.note: Use on the outskirts of, not in the outskirts of.

items.example: The town has a busy market square.
items.note: Generally smaller than a city; town can also refer to its central area.

items.example: We usually meet in the centre of town.
items.note: British English: centre; American English: center.

items.example: Their office is in the centre.
items.note: Contrast in the centre with on the outskirts.

items.example: We moved last spring.
items.note: Move can mean change your home or place of residence.

items.example: They decided to move to a quieter town.
items.note: Use move to + destination when changing where you live.

items.example: I used to live near the station.
items.note: Used to + base verb describes a past situation that is no longer true.

items.example: Our present flat has a small balcony.
items.note: Present is an adjective meaning current, not a gift in this context.

items.example: There's plenty of space for the children to play.
items.note: Space is generally uncountable when it means available room.

items.example: The new flat gives us more space.
items.note: Use more, not many, with uncountable space.

items.pt: vista; paisagem vista de um lugar
items.example: There's a lovely view from the kitchen window.
items.note: The scene you can see from a particular place.

items.example: The upstairs rooms have nice views of the hills.
items.note: A natural plural expression for attractive scenery seen from a property.

items.example: They rent a small flat in Manchester.
items.note: The usual British English word; apartment is common in American English.

items.example: She's looking for an apartment near the university.
items.note: Common in American English and increasingly used in British English.

items.example: We rent rather than own our home.
items.note: As a verb, rent means pay to use a property you do not own.

items.example: It's expensive to rent a flat near the centre.
items.note: Rent and own describe different arrangements for living in a property.

items.pt: no andar de cima; lá em cima
items.example: My neighbours upstairs have two children.
items.note: Can describe location or movement to a higher floor.

items.pt: no andar de baixo; lá embaixo
items.example: The family downstairs has a friendly dog.
items.note: Can describe location or movement to a lower floor.

items.example: There are twenty homes in that block of flats.
items.note: British English term for a building containing several separate flats.

items.example: The building looks modern, but it is quite old.
items.note: Describes a style or design associated with the present or recent times.

items.example: The lift is out of order today.
items.note: British English: lift; American English: elevator.

items.example: We can take the lift to the sixth floor.
items.note: Take the lift means travel in an elevator.

items.example: The apartment has air conditioning for summer.
items.note: A system that cools the air inside a room or building.

items.example: Their office is on a higher floor.
items.note: A floor may mean a level of a building or the surface you walk on.

items.example: The reception desk is on the ground floor.
items.note: In British English, the level at street level is the ground floor.

items.example: Our friends live on the first floor.
items.note: In British English, the first floor is one level above the ground floor.

items.example: My office is on the second floor.
items.note: Use on before floor numbers: on the second floor.

items.example: They have a quiet flat on the top floor.
items.note: The highest occupied level of a building.

items.example: The meeting room is on the second floor.
items.note: Use on the + ordinal number + floor, not in the second floor.

items.example: We eat breakfast on the balcony in summer.
items.note: An outdoor platform attached to an upper floor.

items.pt: porta da frente; porta de entrada
items.example: Someone left a parcel outside the front door.
items.note: The main entrance door to a house or flat.

items.example: There are five steps up to the entrance.
items.note: Steps are individual rises in a staircase; distinct from stairs as a whole.

items.example: I normally use the stairs instead of the lift.
items.note: Plural stairs refers to a set of steps connecting levels.

items.pt: usar a escada; subir ou descer pela escada
items.example: Let's take the stairs for some exercise.
items.note: A common alternative to taking the lift.

items.example: Our neighbours live on the third floor.
items.note: Ordinal floor expression practised in the exercises; British numbering applies.

items.section: C · A house in the country
items.example: My grandparents own a small house.
items.note: Own means possess something rather than rent it.

items.pt: ter casa própria; ser dono de uma casa
items.section: C · A house in the country
items.example: They hope to own a house one day.
items.note: Contrast own a house with rent a house.

items.section: C · A house in the country
items.example: They spent the weekend in a stone cottage.
items.note: Usually a small house, often old and associated with the countryside.

items.section: C · A house in the country
items.example: Her parents live in the country.
items.note: Here country means a rural area, not a nation.

items.section: C · A house in the country
items.example: It's a charming little cottage near the river.
items.note: An approving adjective meaning pleasantly attractive.

items.pt: caráter; personalidade própria de um lugar
items.section: C · A house in the country
items.example: The old house has character despite its small rooms.
items.note: For a building, character means distinctive and interesting qualities.

items.pt: ter muita personalidade; ter muito charme
items.section: C · A house in the country
items.example: This unusual cottage has lots of character.
items.note: A positive way to describe a distinctive building.

items.section: C · A house in the country
items.example: The hallway is dark because it has no windows.
items.note: Opposite: light, when discussing the amount of daylight.

items.section: C · A house in the country
items.example: The large windows make the room light.
items.note: Here light is an adjective opposite to dark; it does not mean lightweight.

items.section: C · A house in the country
items.example: It takes a while to heat the whole house.
items.note: Heat as a verb means make a room, building or substance warm.

items.section: C · A house in the country
items.example: This old building is difficult to heat in winter.
items.note: A useful adjective + infinitive pattern for homes.

items.section: C · A house in the country
items.example: The central heating comes on before sunrise.
items.note: A system that heats several rooms in a building.

items.section: C · A house in the country
items.example: The cottage has no central heating, so we use a stove.
items.note: Use no + noun phrase to express the absence of a feature.

units.title: Unit 18 — Around the home
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 18. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Daily life · Rooms and household objects
learningObjectives: Identify common rooms, including an en-suite bathroom, a spare room, a study and a utility room.
Describe sharing a bedroom and having your own room.
Recognise household appliances and kitchen items from the labelled illustration and exercises.
Distinguish a kitchen sink from a bathroom washbasin.
Describe furniture, cushions, rugs, carpets, curtains and blinds.
Describe bedding with duvet, sheet, blanket and pillow.
Express preferences and distinguish similar household objects and materials.

items.example: They stayed in a one-bedroom flat for a year.
items.note: Hyphenate number + bedroom when it modifies a noun.

items.example: We moved into a four-bedroom house last autumn.
items.note: Use bedroom in the singular inside this compound modifier.

items.example: My bedroom faces the garden.
items.note: A room used for sleeping.

items.example: We usually have breakfast in the kitchen.
items.note: A room where meals are prepared.

items.example: Everyone gathered in the living room after dinner.
items.note: A room for sitting, relaxing and spending time together.

items.example: There's a small bathroom next to the bedroom.
items.note: A room with facilities for washing, usually including a bath or shower.

items.example: The twins share a bedroom while the house is being renovated.
items.note: Share means use the same thing as another person.

items.pt: dividir um cômodo; dividir um quarto
items.example: I used to share a room with my younger brother.
items.note: Use share a room with someone, not share a room to someone.

items.example: The guest bedroom has an en-suite bathroom.
items.note: An en-suite bathroom is connected directly to a bedroom.

items.pt: com banheiro privativo; integrado ao quarto
items.example: We booked a double room with an en-suite shower.
items.note: Often written en-suite before a noun and en suite after one.

items.example: Their teenage son has his own study space.
items.note: Teenage refers to ages thirteen through nineteen.

items.pt: seu próprio quarto; quarto só seu
items.example: Each child would like their own room.
items.note: Own emphasises that something is not shared with another person.

items.example: Our spare room is ready for visitors.
items.note: An additional room that is not normally used as the main bedroom.

items.example: We have two guests staying this weekend.
items.note: A person invited to stay or visit; not the same as host.

items.pt: no andar de baixo; lá embaixo
items.example: The dining room is downstairs.
items.note: Used for the lower level of a home; also featured in Unit 17.

items.example: We keep the large table in the dining room.
items.note: A room specifically intended for eating meals.

items.example: She works from home in a quiet study.
items.note: As a noun, a study can mean a room for reading or working.

items.example: The fridge-freezer is beside the kitchen door.
items.note: A single appliance with both refrigeration and freezing compartments.

items.example: We replaced our old cooker last month.
items.note: British English: an appliance used to cook food; often includes a hob and oven.

items.example: The bread is in the oven.
items.note: An enclosed part of a cooker used for baking or roasting.

items.example: Put the dirty plates in the dishwasher.
items.note: An appliance used to wash dishes automatically.

items.example: The washing machine is in the utility room.
items.note: A small room for practical household jobs and appliances.

items.example: The washing machine finishes in ten minutes.
items.note: An appliance for washing clothes, not dishes.

items.example: Warm the soup in the microwave.
items.note: Often short for microwave oven.

items.example: Turn off the tap after washing your hands.
items.note: British English tap; American English faucet.

items.example: I'll boil some water in the kettle.
items.note: A container or electrical appliance for heating water.

items.example: We chose blue tiles for the kitchen wall.
items.note: Hard pieces of material used to cover floors or walls.

items.example: The frozen vegetables are in the freezer.
items.note: A compartment or appliance kept below freezing temperature.

items.example: There are clean glasses in the cupboard.
items.note: The spelling contains a silent p; cupboards is the plural.

items.example: The kitchen cupboards need cleaning.
items.note: Plural of cupboard; common for built-in kitchen storage.

items.example: Please leave the dirty dishes in the sink.
items.note: Normally used for a kitchen basin.

items.example: The washbasin in the bathroom is cracked.
items.note: Normally used for the basin in a bathroom; basin is also common.

items.example: There's a mirror above the basin.
items.note: Basin is often short for washbasin in bathroom contexts.

items.example: Put the milk back in the fridge.
items.note: Informal short form of refrigerator.

items.example: You have a choice of colours for the curtains.
items.note: A choice is a decision between different possibilities.

items.pt: uma variedade de; uma escolha entre
items.example: They offered us a choice of three designs.
items.note: Use a choice of + plural countable noun for several options.

items.example: I prefer the darker curtains.
items.note: Prefer A to B when comparing two things.

items.example: The sofa is big enough for three people.
items.note: A long soft seat for more than one person.

items.example: These soft cushions make the chair comfortable.
items.note: Opposite of firm in descriptions of furniture.

items.example: I prefer a firm mattress.
items.note: For furniture, firm means supportive and not very soft.

items.example: Grandad fell asleep in his favourite armchair.
items.note: A comfortable chair designed for one person, usually with arms.

items.example: She added a cushion to the armchair.
items.note: A soft pad used on a sofa, chair or floor.

items.example: The living room has a wooden floor.
items.note: Wooden describes what the floor is made from.

items.example: There is a rug beside the bed.
items.note: A floor covering that usually does not cover the whole room.

items.pt: carpete; tapete que cobre o piso
items.example: The bedroom has a thick carpet.
items.note: Often covers most or all of a floor; contrast with rug.

items.example: We close the curtains when it gets dark.
items.note: Fabric panels covering a window; usually plural.

items.example: The blinds let some daylight into the room.
items.note: Adjustable window coverings that differ from fabric curtains.

items.example: I use a light duvet in summer.
items.note: A thick, filled bed covering, often used instead of sheets and blankets.

items.example: There's a clean sheet on the bed.
items.note: A large thin cloth used on a bed.

items.example: She put a warm blanket over her knees.
items.note: A separate covering used for warmth.

items.example: I need another pillow to sleep comfortably.
items.note: Supports the head when sleeping; distinct from cushion.

items.example: We're going to put down a carpet in the hall.
items.note: Here put down means lay or install a floor covering.

items.example: She heated the sauce in a saucepan.
items.note: A deep cooking pan with one long handle.

items.example: The cup comes with a matching saucer.
items.note: A small plate placed under a cup.

items.example: The spare bedroom has a small shower room.
items.note: A bathroom containing a shower; it may not have a bathtub.
